segments.text: The Qur'an describes the sun and the moon with one strange verb. Not shining... not rising. Swimming. And the longer you sit with that word... the better it gets.
segments._shot: sun flaring low over an ocean horizon

segments.text: This is the verse... of the swimmers.
segments.title: YASBAHUN
segments._shot: slow star-trail circles on deep black

segments.text: Seventh century Arabia had no telescopes. The sky most people imagined was a fixed dome... lights pinned to it, wheeling around a still earth. Into that world came sentences that moved everything.
segments._shot: ancient stone sundial or still desert monoliths at night

segments.text: And it is He who created the night and the day, and the sun and the moon... all in an orbit... swimming.
segments._shot: the moon gliding slowly behind thin clouds

segments.text: And again, in the chapter Ya-Sin... It is not allowable for the sun to reach the moon, nor does the night overtake the day... but each, in an orbit, is swimming. The Arabic verb is yasbahun... they swim, they glide... each body carried along its own invisible lane.
segments._shot: timelapse of sun and moon paths across a wide sky

segments.text: Today we know the moon glides around the earth... the earth around the sun... the sun itself around the galaxy... nothing in the sky is nailed anywhere. Everything floats along a path. The classical scholars did not know the physics... they simply trusted the verb. And the verb held.
segments._shot: slow drift through a dense starfield

segments.text: Order without pillars... lanes without collisions... for billions of years. The verse does not ask you to be an astronomer. It asks you to ask... who is holding all of this in its lanes?
segments._shot: serene full night sky over mountains, immense
